# Results — Study 132 (Yield-Curve-Steepener) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — long TLT when
the prior-day 10Y-minus-3M Treasury slope is positive (steep curve), flat (cash) otherwise —
tested against **unconditional buy-and-hold TLT** as the null. Inference via Newey-West HAC
t-stat on per-day returns; block-bootstrap 95% CI on the annualised Sharpe. No look-ahead:
the slope on day *t* forms the signal; TLT return is from close *t* to close *t+1*. As-of
**2026-06-14**.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Source | Window | Fingerprint (TLT_close) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLT, IEF, SHY, ^TNX, ^IRX | Yahoo Finance daily | 2002-07-31 → 2026-06-12 | `47f49f57ea8d` |

- **n = 6,000** trading days (~23.8 years).
- Slope = TNX − IRX (10Y minus 3M Treasury, in percentage points).
- Slope mean = **+1.42 pp** (steep most of the time), std = 1.27 pp.
- Curve was steep (slope > 0) on **86.5%** of days; inverted/flat on **13.5%**.
- Longest inversion: ~503 trading days (2022-24 episode).

## The central test — Q5 vs Q1 quintile spread

Days are ranked into five slope-quintiles (rolling 252-day out-of-sample percentile).
Q5 = steepest curve, Q1 = most inverted. Forward TLT log-returns are computed for
each quintile at horizons of 1, 5, and 21 business days.

### Quintile mean forward 1-day TLT returns

| Quintile | Description | n | mean (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Q1 | Most inverted | 2,105 | **+1.71** | +1.01 |
| Q2 | Moderately inverted | 596 | **−2.18** | −0.52 |
| Q3 | Near flat | 631 | **−2.81** | −0.84 |
| Q4 | Moderately steep | 892 | **+0.70** | +0.25 |
| Q5 | Steepest | 1,713 | **+4.09** | +1.82 |

**Q5−Q1 spread = +2.37 bps/day, HAC *t* = +0.64.** The direction is right (Q5 > Q1)
but the pattern is non-monotone (Q2 and Q3 fall below Q1), and the spread is far below
the inference bar of 2.

### Q5-Q1 spread across horizons

| Horizon | Q5 mean | Q1 mean | spread | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 day | +4.09 bps | +1.71 bps | **+2.37 bps** | +0.64 |
| 5 day | +13.06 bps | +8.27 bps | **+4.79 bps** | +0.22 |
| 21 day | +50.93 bps | +30.62 bps | **+20.31 bps** | +0.34 |

Longer-horizon spreads are larger in absolute magnitude but lower in t-statistic once
HAC accounts for the autocorrelation in overlapping 5- and 21-day returns. None clears
the bar.

## The timing overlay vs buy-and-hold

The binary rule: long TLT when prior-day slope > 0, flat otherwise. Pin against
unconditional buy-and-hold TLT. Cost: 2 bps per switch.

| Arm | n | mean (bps/day) | ann. Sharpe | HAC *t* | switches/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Buy-and-hold TLT (passive)** | 5,999 | **+1.43** | **+0.252** | +1.35 | — |
| Steep-curve timer (active, 2 bps) | 5,999 | **+1.31** | **+0.250** | +1.37 | ~1.7 |
| Active − passive spread | — | **−0.12** | — | **−0.27** | — |

- The timing rule's Sharpe (**0.250**) is virtually identical to buy-and-hold (**0.252**).
- The active-minus-passive spread is **−0.12 bps/day** (HAC *t* = −0.27) — noise.
- Block-bootstrap 95% CI on the active arm: **[−0.128, +0.618]** (9.1% of resamples < 0).
- Even at zero cost the active arm underperforms: spread at 0 bps cost = −0.11 bps/day.

## Regime statistics

| Regime | n | n% | mean bps/day | Sharpe (ann) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Full sample | 5,998 | 100% | +1.42 | +0.250 | +1.34 |
| Steep curve (slope > 0) | 5,190 | 86.5% | +1.53 | +0.271 | +1.38 |
| Flat/inverted (slope ≤ 0) | 808 | 13.5% | +0.72 | +0.121 | +0.22 |

The steep-curve sub-sample Sharpe (+0.271) is modestly better than the full sample
(+0.250) and materially better than the inverted sub-sample (+0.121). But:
- The inverted-curve sub-sample is too small (808 days, 13.5%) to be individually
  significant (HAC *t* = 0.22 vs zero for TLT returns).
- The steep sub-sample is itself only barely significant (HAC *t* = 1.38 vs zero).
- The difference between the two sub-samples is directionally right but far from robust.

## Cost sweep (active arm)

| Round-trip cost | active mean (bps/day) | active Sharpe | vs passive Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | +1.32 | +0.252 | ≈ 0.000 |
| 1.0 bps | +1.32 | +0.251 | −0.001 |
| 2.0 bps | +1.31 | +0.250 | −0.002 |
| 5.0 bps | +1.29 | +0.246 | −0.006 |

At ~1.7 switches/year, each bp of cost reduces the active Sharpe by only ~0.003/year —
costs are not the killer here. The gross underperformance is the problem: even at zero
cost the active Sharpe trails buy-and-hold.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery works when there's something to find

A synthetic tape with tunable slope-to-TLT signal (slope_signal > 0 plants a genuine
relationship between steep curve and forward TLT returns):

| Planted slope_signal | Q5-Q1 spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | Beats null? |
|---|--:|--:|:--:|
| 0.000 (null) | ~5 | ~2 | no (within noise) |
| 0.005 | ~32 | ~11 | yes |
| 0.012 | ~105 | ~36 | yes |
| Real tape | +2.37 | +0.64 | **no** |

The real-tape spread sits at the low end of the planted-signal distribution, consistent
with a very small (possibly zero) true effect, not a confirmed signal.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The Q5−Q1 spread at 1-day horizon is +2.37 bps/day (HAC *t* = +0.64).
  The direction is right but the pattern is non-monotone and all t-statistics sit well
  below 2 across all horizons tested. "WEAK" reflects a hint of the claimed effect at
  insufficient statistical power, not a confirmed signal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The timing overlay trails buy-and-hold at every cost level.
  Active Sharpe 0.250 vs passive 0.252; spread *t* = −0.27. With only ~1.7 switches/year,
  costs are negligible — the gross underperformance is the problem.
- **Beats buy-and-hold? — No.** Spread −0.12 bps/day, *t* = −0.27. The inverted-curve
  regime is too rare (13.5%) and the in-regime TLT performance is too heterogeneous
  to achieve a reliable timing advantage.
